newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais says no decision on cash needs.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais says no decision on cash needs.

text.p: French bank Credit Lyonnais denied on Thursday a report it was seeking a 12 billion franc ($2.3 billion) state capital injection to ready it for privatisation, saying no decision had been made yet on how much cash it would need.
"The amount is not yet possible to calculate," a spokesman for the state-controlled bank said, rejecting a report in London's Financial Times that Credit Lyonnais was calling for 12 billion francs.
"What we know is Credit Lyonnais has a tier one capital ratio of 4.5 percent while privatised banks have a higher ratio," he said.
He said it was clear the tier one ratio -- an international banking solvency measure -- needed to be raised to attract a buyer or buyers but "it is not possible to say to what level".
"Given the bank's commitments," it would cost eight billion francs to raise the ratio by one percentage point, he added.

The conservative government said last month it would stage a third bailout of Credit Lyonnais, whose plight ranks as France's worst banking horror story, to ready it for sale. The only question is how much it will have to inject into the bank.
The Financial Times quoted on Thursday bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade as saying the bank needed a 12 billion franc state recapitalisation to boost its balance sheet ahead of its sale.
He was reported to have said the bank, whose woes stem from an expansion spree in the 1980s that nearly made it bankrupt, needed the money to raise its tier one capital to six percent.

Last week, when he released the bank's results showing a 67 million franc first half profit, he suggested the bank's ratio might need to be raised to 5.5 percent and that could cost eight to nine billion francs.

But the day after, banking analysts quoted him as telling them such a level might be a "little tight" and a 6.0 or 6.5 percent tier one ratio might be needed. Bank officials have said, however, he was only been conjecturing about scenarios.
The average tier one ratio for French banks is six percent while it is seven percent for the European sector as a whole.

The government has said it wants to privatise Credit Lyonnais as soon as possible but the bank has said a sale will likely not be possible until mid-1998. The bank is drawing up a privatisation plan to present by year end.

Meanwhile, the finance ministry said it had no comment on Credit Lyonnais's potential cash needs or the time frame for its privatisation. But a finance ministry official said it was natural Peyrelevade "should start advancing hypotheses".

The recapitalisation would be on top of 3.9 billion francs of emergency state aid announced last month to repair what turned out to be overly harsh terms of a state salvage last year that would have driven the bank back into the red.
In what was seen as a quid pro quo for winning the European Commission's approval for fresh state aid, the government accelerated the bank's privatisation from the year 2000.
